author: Ben Jonson
title: The Fox’s gold, song and sentence
about: Volpone, a rich Venetian with no heir, pretends to be dying so that men who hope to inherit will bring him gifts, and his servant Mosca lets each think he is the heir. In the first passage Volpone greets his gold. In the second he sings to Celia, whose husband has left her alone with him in hope of the inheritance. In the third a judge closes the trial at which Volpone, Mosca and the three men they cheated have been sentenced, and Volpone steps forward to the audience.

view.says: One remark by Auden on this play was found. In conversation that Alan Ansen noted down in his entry for January 8, 1947, he said he had a special liking for *The Alchemist* and *Bartholomew Fair*, and found *Volpone* too unpleasant. Of Jonson’s comedies as a group he wrote that they are classical where Shakespeare’s are Christian. Christian comedy ends with its people exposed and forgiven, classical comedy with its people exposed and punished.
view.quote: In classical comedy the characters are exposed and punished: when the curtain falls, the audience is laughing and those on stage are in tears.
view.source: “The Globe,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 177; Alan Ansen, *The Table Talk of W. H. Auden*, edited by Nicholas Jenkins (1991), p. 18

plates.heading: Volpone to his gold: the first lines of the scene

lenses.label: Word

notes.gloss: a saint’s casket · Latin scrinium, chest
notes.note: From Latin *scrinium*, a case or chest for books or papers. The Oxford dictionary quotes these first two lines among figurative uses, where a person or thing is venerated or idolized.
Later in the speech he calls the gold *dear saint* again, and in Act 3 Bonario, who frees Celia from him, speaks of *this altar* and calls Volpone’s treasure *dross* and his *idol*.
The dictionary gives it as the English for Latin *ave*, and *Hail Mary* as the angel’s greeting to Mary and the prayer, *Ave Maria*.
After Latin *anima mundi*, the early philosophers’ name for the principle that animates the world.
The Ram is the constellation of the zodiac that the sun enters in March: on the 21st, by the dictionary’s reckoning.
In alchemy *Sol*, the sun, was the name for gold.
Latin *adorare* is to address, salute or reverence, and in late Latin to worship.
From Latin *reliquiae*, remains: a part of a saint’s body or belongings, kept and venerated.

lenses.caption: Volpone addresses his gold in words of Christian worship. It is his Saint. He greets it with Hail, the greeting that begins the prayer to Mary. He asks to kiss it with adoration, and each relick of the hoard besides, which he calls sacred treasure in a blessed room. A shrine was the casket of a saint’s relics. Auden wrote that the basic pattern of Jonson’s comedy of humors is the morality play with one of the seven deadly sins made its hero. A humor was a person’s temperament, his habitual bent. A morality play had qualities such as virtues and vices for its chief persons. The hero of this comedy begins Act 1 by worshipping money.
lenses.why: Volpone greets his gold in the words of Christian worship, saint, hail, adoration, relic, shrine, so Act 1 opens on a man worshipping money; Auden says a Jonson hero is one of the seven deadly sins.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage and what its lines say; the speech in full, with *dear saint*, is in [Act 1, Scene 1](#/read/volpone/a1s1:5). *A New English Dictionary*, under Shrine, Saint, Hail, Hail Mary, Soul, Teeming, Aries, Chaos, Centre, Sol, Adoration, Adore, Relic, Sacred, Blessed, Morality and Humour. Bonario’s altar and idol: [Act 3, Scene 6](#/read/volpone/a3s6:128). Auden, “The Globe,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 173.

lenses.label: Sentence
lenses.caption: The sentence starts with what he is, more glad, and keeps back who is glad. First comes the comparison: the teeming earth sees the sun enter the Ram, as it does in March. Verb and subject come three lines later: Am I. Keeping back the main words holds a hearer in suspense, which throws the emphasis on the words waited for. The earth’s gladness at the longed-for sun is told in full; then the speaker outdoes it. What gladdens him is the gold’s splendour darkening his, and his is the sun’s. Then the gold is likened to a flame at night and to the day struck out of chaos.
lenses.why: The sentence keeps back its verb and subject, Am I, for three lines and fills the wait with the earth’s gladness at the longed-for sun, so that gladness is told first and then outdone by a man looking at gold.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage: the order of the sentence’s parts, and the three lines from *more glad* to *Am I*. What the lines say. Suspense, the emphasis it throws on the words waited for, and the adjective set before its subject: Edwin A. Abbott, *How to Write Clearly* (1883), rules 30 and 33. The Ram and *teeming*: *A New English Dictionary*, under Aries and Teeming.

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.meterName: blank verse: ten syllables and five beats, the line beginning off the beat

5.5.voice: / x x / x / x x x /

points.say: The greeting to the day: six syllables, three of them unstressed and in a row.
The greeting to the gold: six syllables, four stresses. Two of them meet at *world’s soul*.
The first beat falls on *I*, which the sentence has kept back for three lines.

lenses.caption: These lines are blank verse: ten syllables to the line, a beat on every second one, and no pattern of rhyme. One line, ending relick, runs a syllable past the last beat. Volpone gives two greetings of six syllables. In Good morning to the day three unstressed syllables run together before day. Hail the world’s soul, and mine has four stresses: it starts on one, against the measure, and at world’s soul two stand together, which slows the line. He names the gold second and gives it the heavier, slower greeting.
lenses.why: Volpone greets the day and then the gold in six syllables each: the gold’s greeting has four stresses, more than the day’s, and two stand side by side, so the line slows on the gold’s name, the world’s soul.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage: the measure of each line, the stresses of the two greetings, the beat on *I*. What the lines say. Blank verse, the extra syllable at a line’s end, and the slowing of a line when a stress is crowded in where the measure has no beat: Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification* (1922), chapters 4 and 5.

rows.text: Mosca withdraws the curtain, and discovers piles of gold, plate, jewels, etc.

plates.heading: Volpone’s song to Celia: lines 1 to 10 and 15 to 18

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: The song is in short couplets: lines of four beats, rhymed in pairs. The quick return of the rhyme makes each pair a unit, and the short line, so often repeated, gives an effect of hurry. Hurry is what the song urges: love while we can. Twice a pair is split: its second line starts a statement that runs through the next pair. The first is the three lines on suns, light and night, taken from the Latin poet Catullus. The second is the rule that closes the song, where the split pair rhymes steal with reveal, the act with its discovery. One sound picks out four words of the rule: sin, steal, sweet, seen.
lenses.why: The song is in short rhymed pairs, a form that gives an effect of hurry, and hurry is what it urges; the pair split at the closing rule rhymes steal with reveal, the act with its discovery.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and a count of the nine rhymed pairs of the whole song in [Act 3, Scene 6](#/read/volpone/a3s6:106): two are split. The short couplet, its hurry, and the repeated first sound: Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification* (1922), chapters 4 and 5. The lines on suns: Catullus, poem 5, lines 4 to 6, in E. T. Merrill’s edition (1893).

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: From Latin *probare*, to test: to *prove* a thing was to make trial of it, and so to know it by experience.
Line 4 of Catullus’s poem says that suns can set and come back.
In Catullus it is one unbroken night that must be slept through.
In Catullus all of it is to be valued at one *as*, a copper coin.
Latin poets called a stolen or secret love a theft, *furtum*, mostly in the plural; Virgil’s *Georgics* has *dulcia furta*, the sweet thefts of Mars.
In Act 4 the lawyer Voltore tells the court, falsely, that Celia has been *taken in the act* with Bonario, the man who freed her.
Latin *crimen* is first a charge or accusation, then the offense charged.

lenses.caption: The song is made from a Latin poem, Catullus’s to Lesbia, which opens with a call to live and love. Jonson’s suns that set and rise are Catullus’s soles, his perpetual night is nox perpetua, and rumour is the rumores, the talk of stern old men, which Catullus values at one copper coin. Catullus goes on to count kisses. This song turns to watchers: the four lines left out here ask whether spies and a man’s ears cannot be deceived. The closing rule is not in Catullus’s poem. Latin poets called secret loves thefts, furta, and the rule carries the figure through: steal, thefts, taken, crimes.
lenses.why: The song takes its call to love, its suns, its perpetual night and its idle talk from Catullus; where he counts kisses it turns to spies and a rule on being caught, in the words of theft.
lenses.stands: Catullus, poem 5, in E. T. Merrill’s edition (1893), set beside the song; Wikipedia, “Catullus 5,” on Jonson’s use of the poem. Lewis and Short, *A Latin Dictionary*, under *sol*, *brevis*, *lux*, *nox*, *perpetuus*, *rumor*, *as*, *furtum* and *crimen*. Virgil, *Georgics* 4.346. *A New English Dictionary*, under Prove, Loose, Toy, Take and Crime. The four lines left out: [the whole song](#/read/volpone/a3s6:106). The lawyer’s charge: [Act 4, Scene 2](#/read/volpone/a4s2:96).

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: antithesis
lenses.plain: two opposed things set side by side, often in phrases of the same build
lenses.caption: The last four lines are an antithesis. On one side is the act: to steal love’s fruits is no sin. On the other is being found out: to reveal the theft, to be taken or seen, these are the crimes. Celia’s husband has argued the same way earlier in the scene, asking who shall know it. Before the scene ends Bonario rushes in to free her, and Volpone cries that he is unmasked and undone. In the last scene he throws off his own disguise. Auden says that classical comedy ends with its people exposed and punished.
lenses.why: The song’s last four lines set the act against its discovery: stealing is no sin, being revealed, taken or seen is the crime; before the scene ends Volpone is unmasked, and Auden says classical comedy exposes and punishes its people.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. Antithesis as *A New English Dictionary* defines it. Corvino’s question: [earlier in the scene](#/read/volpone/a3s6:24). Bonario’s entrance and Volpone’s cry: [after the song](#/read/volpone/a3s6:128). The disguise thrown off: [Act 5, Scene 8](#/read/volpone/a5s8:189). Auden, “The Globe,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 177.

lenses.label: Beat
lenses.meterName: seven syllables and four beats, the line beginning on a beat

points.say: *love’s* can also be said lightly; the line then keeps every stress on a beat.
Two stresses together: the line slows here.
Seven syllables, two of them stressed.

lenses.caption: The measure is seven syllables and four beats, the line beginning on a beat. Six lines of Ariel’s song in The Tempest keep the same one. Two lines, ending ever and sever, run a syllable past the last beat. In the ten lines shown first the voice can keep every stress on a beat; in the closing rule it cannot. At sweet thefts two stresses stand together, and a stressed word crowded in where the measure has no beat slows the line. The line after has only two stresses, on taken and seen. A line short of stresses turns attention to the words that keep them. Those two words name what the rule calls crimes.
lenses.why: For ten lines the song’s stresses can all fall on its four beats; in the closing rule two stresses meet at sweet thefts and slow the line, and the next line keeps only two, on taken and seen, the crime.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. The measure of Ariel’s song: the first passage of [the page on *The Tempest*](#/tempest). The slowing of a line where two stresses meet, and the attention that a line short of stresses turns on its important words: Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification* (1922), chapter 5. What the last two lines say.

plates.heading: The court’s last words and the Fox’s

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: The judge’s speech has no rhyme until its last two lines, feed and bleed. On Shakespeare’s stage rhyme was often used to end a scene, and Acts 2 and 3 of this play end on a rhymed pair. This pair ends the trial, and the court goes out. Then the Fox comes forward and speaks six lines, all in rhymed pairs. Each rhyme joins a word of his case to a word of the audience: laws with applause, due with you, stands with hands. The court has judged him, and in these rhymes he puts his case to the audience, to censure him or to clap.
lenses.why: The judge’s speech rhymes only in its last two lines, feed and bleed, as rhyme often closed a scene on that stage; the Fox’s three rhymes then join each word of his case to a word of the audience.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and [the directions printed between the two speeches](#/read/volpone/a5s8:266). Rhyme used to end a scene: E. A. Abbott, *A Shakespearian Grammar* (1870), paragraph 515. The rhymed pairs that end [Act 2](#/read/volpone/a2s3:98) and [Act 3](#/read/volpone/a3s6:254) in the text printed here. What the Fox’s six lines say.

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: simile
lenses.plain: a comparison that says one thing is like another
lenses.caption: The judge’s last sentence says that Mischiefs, wrongs, feed like beasts till they are fat, and then bleed, which could mean to die by bloodshed. Volpone has used these words before. In the first scene he boasts that he does not fat beasts to feed the shambles, the slaughterhouse, and calls his visitors birds of prey who think him a carcass. One scene before this he says that unless a vein is closed he and Mosca bleed dead. He speaks next, and calls himself the Fox.
lenses.why: The judge’s closing simile, wrongs that feed like beasts till fat and then bleed, uses Volpone’s own words: fat, beasts and feed from the first scene, bleed from the scene before, and he speaks next as the Fox.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. *A New English Dictionary*, under Simile, Mischief, Bleed and Shamble. Volpone’s boast that he fats no beasts, and his birds of prey: [Act 1, Scene 1](#/read/volpone/a1s1:9) and [later in that scene](#/read/volpone/a1s1:83). *Bleed dead*: [Act 5, Scene 7](#/read/volpone/a5s7:3).

lenses.label: Word

notes.gloss: the song’s word for being seen
notes.note: In Act 3 Volpone sang that to be revealed, taken or seen is what is counted a crime.
To *reward* was to repay, for good or for ill; in Act 3 Bonario, freeing Celia, says that Volpone shall meet his *just reward*.
The word meant an injury or evil-doing, and also a person who does harm: in Act 5 Volpone calls Mosca his *witty mischief*.
The Prologue speaks of the *palates* of the season, and says the poet’s ink keeps only a little *salt*, to rub the audience’s cheeks red with laughter.
An Italian dictionary of 1611 gives *volpone* as an old fox, and also an old, crafty, subtle, sneaking companion.
An evil deed or crime was the commonest sense of the word in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries; in Act 4 the lawyer calls the adultery he alleges *this foul fact*.
A few speeches earlier the judge tells Volpone that a gentleman cannot fall under *like censure*, meaning a sentence like Mosca’s.
To *fare* was to get on, and also to be fed, as the rich man in the Bible of 1611 *fared sumptuously every day*; *fare well* was the wish at parting.
*Jovial* also meant under the influence of the planet Jupiter, held to be the source of joy; before his song Volpone says he is in *jovial plight*.

lenses.caption: The Fox uses words of the table and of the court. Applause is a play’s seasoning, and fare meant to feed as well as to get on. A fact was a deed, most often a crime, and to censure could mean to pass sentence: the judge used the word of Mosca’s punishment. In the letter printed before the play Jonson grants that his ending may meet with censure by the strict law of comedy, and answers that the ancients’ comedies do not always end in joy and that a comic poet must imitate justice. Auden calls Jonson’s comedies classical, and says classical comedy ends with its people exposed and punished.
lenses.why: The Fox’s word to the audience, censure, is the court’s word for a sentence and Jonson’s word, in the letter before the play, for what strict comedy may say of an ending that punishes, as Auden says classical comedy does.
lenses.stands: *A New English Dictionary*, under Fact, Censure, Seasoning, Fare, Reward, Mischief, Bleed, Doubtful and Jovial; the glossary of the Project Gutenberg text, under Fact and Censure. The judge’s *censure*: [earlier in the scene](#/read/volpone/a5s8:246). Jonson on his ending: [the Epistle](#/read/volpone/epistle:3). The palates and the salt: [the Prologue](#/read/volpone/prologue:0). John Florio, *Queen Anna’s New World of Words* (1611), under *Volpone*. Auden, “The Globe,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 177.

lenses.caption: The five persons the court sentences have creatures’ names, which an Italian dictionary of Jonson’s day explains. Volpone is an old fox, Mosca a fly, Voltore a vulture, Corbaccio a filthy great raven, Corvino of a raven’s nature. A medieval book of beasts tells how the fox shams death until birds settle on it, then eats them. Each bird brings the Fox a gift in hope of his estate: a piece of plate, gold coin, a pearl, a diamond. Auden describes what happens in a comedy by Jonson: a rascal with brains cheats a fool with money, and the fool deserves it, since he wants nothing more moral than the rascal does. The court punishes all five.
lenses.why: Three birds of prey bring gifts to a fox they take for carrion, and the fox and his fly take the gifts; the court sentences cheats and cheated alike, and Auden says the fool in a Jonson comedy deserves it.
lenses.stands: John Florio, *Queen Anna’s New World of Words* (1611), under *Volpone*, *Mosca*, *Voltore*, *Corbacchio* and *Corvino*. The Aberdeen Bestiary, folio 16r, in the University of Aberdeen’s translation. The gifts and the hope: [Act 1, Scene 1](#/read/volpone/a1s1:21), and Volpone’s [count of the gifts](#/read/volpone/a1s1:610). The five sentences: [Act 5, Scene 8](#/read/volpone/a5s8:238). *A New English Dictionary*, under Chequeen. Auden, “The Joker in the Pack,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 252.

auden.says: Writing of the Elizabethan playwrights, Auden calls Jonson the one highbrow among them and says his debt to the morality play is greater than his debt to Latin comedy. Remove the morality play’s hero, Everyman, he says, and make a deadly sin, one of the seven, the hero in his place; let the remaining six band together to gain by it. That gives the plan on which Jonson’s comedies of humors are built.

Auden writes that the first sight of Iago and Roderigo together, in *Othello*, shows the situation of a comedy by Jonson: a clever rascal is cheating a rich fool, and the fool deserves it, since he wants nothing more moral than the rogue does. If *Othello* were a comedy, he adds, Roderigo would find out at last and not dare go to law, since the whole truth would make him look ridiculous or shameful.
auden.source: “The Joker in the Pack,” in *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), p. 252

auden.says: In an essay of 1948 Auden describes a type of comedy, invented by the Greeks, which grew, he says, into several kinds, among them the comedy of humors that Jonson wrote. Its target is the man who breaks the common rule, not believing that it binds him. He collides with others who stand as far outside the law as he does, while the law leaves him alone. He suffers; the audience, who do not see themselves in him, do not. His suffering teaches him to keep the law, out of caution if not out of conscience.
auden.source: “The Greeks and Us” (1948), in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), p. 30

caveats: No account of *Volpone* by Auden was found, only one remark made in conversation. What he says here about Jonson’s comedies as a group is set beside these passages by this page; he did not apply it to these lines himself.

His remark that *Volpone* is too unpleasant comes from Alan Ansen’s record of his conversation, not from Auden’s own writing. The book was not seen in full: the words, the page and the date were read in short extracts of a scanned copy.

Some syllables can fairly be stressed another way, among them *Good* in the first line of Act 1, and *no* and *love’s* in the song’s line on sin. The captions rest only on stresses that are not in doubt.

The Oxford dictionary quotes the *shrine* lines among figurative uses of the word for a place of worship; the casket is its older sense. The second senses given for *fare* (to feed) and *mischiefs* (wrongdoers) were in use in Jonson’s time; that he meant both at once is an inference.

The song is shown without its lines 11 to 14. Act and scene numbers are this text’s: the Oxford dictionary cites a line of its Act 1, Scene 1 as Act 1, Scene 3 of Jonson’s folio of 1616, so other editions may number these scenes differently.
